Under the current text of 49 CFR § 395.3(a), the three figures are 10, 14 and 11:

- **Off duty before driving, § 395.3(a)(1):** The required rest before a shift's driving is 10 consecutive hours off duty.
- **On-duty window, § 395.3(a)(2):** The cutoff for driving falls 14 consecutive hours after the driver comes on duty following that 10-hour break.
- **Driving time, § 395.3(a)(3)(i):** Total driving within that 14-hour period is capped at 11 hours.

Exceptions in § 395.1 can modify these limits (for example, short-haul and sleeper-berth provisions).

Under 47 CFR § 97.313:

- **General maximum:** No station may transmit with a transmitter power exceeding **1.5 kW PEP** (1,500 watts peak envelope power) [ecfr.gov](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-47/chapter-I/subchapter-D/part-97/subpart-D/section-97.313).

- **10.10–10.15 MHz segment (30-meter band):** No station may transmit with a transmitter power output exceeding **200 W PEP** (200 watts peak envelope power) [ecfr.gov](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-47/chapter-I/subchapter-D/part-97/subpart-D/section-97.313).

**Measure:** In both cases, the limit is expressed as peak envelope power (PEP), measured at the output of the transmitter, not as RMS power or power input to the antenna [hamstudy.org](https://hamstudy.org/browse/E3_2023/G1C).

Section 97.313(a) also requires that an amateur station use the minimum transmitter power necessary to carry out the desired communications, regardless of these ceilings [law.cornell.edu](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/47/97.313).

Under 49 CFR § 173.120(a), a Class 3 flammable liquid is a liquid with a flash point of **not more than 60 °C (140 °F)**, meaning at or below that figure ([ecfr.gov](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-49/subtitle-B/chapter-I/subchapter-C/part-173/subpart-D/section-173.120)).

The definition also has a second prong. It covers any material in a liquid phase with a flash point **at or above 37.8 °C (100 °F)** that is intentionally heated and offered for transportation or transported at or above its flash point in a bulk packaging ([law.cornell.edu](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/49/173.120)). Both prongs are subject to the exceptions in paragraphs (a)(1)–(5).

One of the search results, [drs.illinois.edu](https://drs.illinois.edu/Page2/Programs/ShippingAndReceivingHazardousMaterials/Definitions), gives the threshold as ≤ 60.5 °C (141 °F) and states the heated-material prong as ≤ 37.8 °C. Both conflict with the current regulatory text, which says 60 °C (140 °F) and "at or above" 37.8 °C.

**Text line (section 4.5.3.1.6): 1000 octets**

- The count includes the terminating `<CRLF>`, leaving 998 octets for content. PHPMailer's SMTP class reflects this with `MAX_LINE_LENGTH = 998`, described as "*excluding* a trailing CRLF break" ([github.com](https://github.com/PHPMailer/PHPMailer/blob/640e68d33218e9886ec700b058613d5552cb31fe/src/SMTP.php)).
- The count does not include the leading dot duplicated for transparency (dot-stuffing).
- The RFC text, as quoted by [improvmx.com](https://improvmx.com/guides/im-getting-a-line-too-long-error/), says the maximum is "1000 octets (not counting the leading dot duplicated for transparency). This number may be increased by the use of SMTP Service Extensions."

**Reply line (section 4.5.3.1.5): 512 octets**

- The count includes the terminating `<CRLF>`. PHPMailer's `MAX_REPLY_LENGTH = 512` is described as "*including* a trailing CRLF line break" ([github.com](https://github.com/PHPMailer/PHPMailer/blob/640e68d33218e9886ec700b058613d5552cb31fe/src/SMTP.php)).
- The count also includes the reply code. This comes from my recollection of the RFC's wording rather than the search results, which only confirm the CRLF.

Both figures match the summary of limits at [rfcinfo.com](http://rfcinfo.com/rfc-5321/4/), which lists the reply line at 512 octets and the text line at 1000 octets.

Extensions can change these limits, as [rfc-editor.org](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5321.html) notes: "extensions can change the minimum limits specified in Section 4.5.3."

Workers in Great Britain are entitled by statute to **5.6 weeks** of paid annual leave per year, capped at **28 days** ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/holiday-entitlement-rights)).

- **How it is calculated:** For a full leave year, the entitlement is the lower of 28 days or 5.6 × the number of days worked per week ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/calculating-holiday-entitlement-for-workers/how-to-calculate-holiday-entitlement-for-workers-on-different-types-of-contract)).
- **Effect of the cap:** The cap only affects people who work more than 5 days a week. Someone working 6 days a week still gets 28 days, not 33.6 ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/calculating-holiday-entitlement-for-workers/how-to-calculate-holiday-entitlement-for-workers-on-different-types-of-contract)).
- **Part-time workers:** They get 5.6 weeks pro rata. For example, someone working 3 days a week gets at least 16.8 days ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/holiday-entitlement-rights)).
- **Bank holidays:** Employers can count these towards the statutory entitlement, but do not have to give them as paid leave ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/holiday-entitlement-rights)).

The entitlement comes from the Working Time Regulations 1998 and covers almost all workers, including agency, irregular-hours and part-year workers ([cipd.org](https://www.cipd.org/uk/knowledge/employment-law/holidays/)). Contracts can give more than this minimum but not less ([london.gov.uk](https://www.london.gov.uk/programmes-strategies/communities-and-social-justice/employment-rights-hub/time-and-leave)).

Under 14 CFR 91.155, the basic VFR minimums in Class E airspace below 10,000 feet MSL are:

- **Flight visibility:** 3 statute miles
- **Distance from clouds:**
  - 500 feet below
  - 1,000 feet above
  - 2,000 feet horizontally

A common memory aid is "3-152" (3 SM, 1,000 above, 500 below, 2,000 horizontal).

For comparison, at or above 10,000 feet MSL in Class E the minimums increase to 5 statute miles visibility, with 1,000 feet below, 1,000 feet above, and 1 statute mile horizontally from clouds.

The 1876 Pocket Manual requires a **two-thirds vote** to adopt a motion for the Previous Question.

Section 20 states it directly: "It shall require a two-thirds vote for its adoption" ([atlas.cs.brown.edu](https://atlas.cs.brown.edu/data/gutenberg/9/0/9/9097/old/7rror10.txt)). This is the 1876 edition that Project Gutenberg carries as EBook #9097 ([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/9097)).

Robert departed deliberately from congressional practice here. He notes that the House of Representatives required only a majority vote for the motion, and the Senate did not allow it at all. He describes the manual's policy as "a mean between those of the House and Senate" ([atlas.cs.brown.edu](https://atlas.cs.brown.edu/data/gutenberg/9/0/9/9097/old/7rror10.txt)).

His reasoning was that in ordinary societies "harmony is so essential, that a two-thirds vote should be required to force the assembly to a final vote without allowing free debate" ([yara.ca](https://www.yara.ca/members/rules/RobertsRulesOfOrderRevised.pdf)).

In the SI Brochure (9th edition, 2019), the luminous efficacy K<sub>cd</sub> is fixed at **683 lm/W** for monochromatic radiation of frequency **540 × 10¹² Hz** (540 THz, green light at a wavelength of about 555 nm).

This is one of the seven defining constants of the SI, and it underpins the definition of the candela.

No, it is not a Class 3 flammable liquid; it is a **combustible liquid** under 49 CFR 173.120(b).

- **Why not Class 3:** Your 65 °C flash point sits just over the Class 3 ceiling of 60 °C (140 °F).
- **What it is:** The band above 60 °C and below 93 °C (200 °F), for liquids outside every other hazard class, carries the "combustible liquid" designation instead.
- **One exit:** Failing to sustain combustion in testing takes such a liquid out of the combustible-liquid requirements altogether.
- **Domestic only:** Shippers can rely on this category only for transport within the United States.

What that means in practice depends on packaging; this part is from my knowledge of 49 CFR 173.150(f) rather than the search results:

- **Non-bulk packaging (450 L / 119 gal or less):** the liquid is not subject to the hazardous materials regulations, unless it is also a hazardous substance, hazardous waste, or marine pollutant.
- **Bulk packaging:** it is regulated, typically shipped as "NA1993, Combustible liquid, n.o.s., PG III" with reduced requirements (shipping papers, marking, and COMBUSTIBLE placards).

The current primary (health-based) PM2.5 standards are:

- **Annual:** 9.0 µg/m³ is the level in force, down from 12.0 µg/m³, and compliance is judged on the annual mean averaged over three years.
- **24-hour:** 35 µg/m³, which the 2024 rule left untouched, and compliance is judged on the 98th percentile averaged over three years.

The annual level is under legal challenge but still stands. Both the industry challenges and EPA's own vacatur request failed at the D.C. Circuit in a June 26, 2026 decision. Supreme Court review was sought by state and industry petitioners on August 28, 2026, and those petitions are still pending, so the 9.0 figure could yet change.

**20 minutes.** A helicopter pilot has to plan for 20 minutes of additional flying at normal cruising speed past the first point of intended landing, under 14 CFR § 91.151(b).

- Time of day makes no difference to that number, unlike the 30-minute day and 45-minute night reserves for airplanes.
- Wind and forecast weather factor into the fuel calculation.
- This is the Part 91 minimum; stricter reserves govern commercial and air carrier flights through separate rules.

From 1 April 2026, the UK rates are:

- **National Living Wage (aged 21 and over):** £12.71 per hour, up 50p (4.1%) from £12.21 ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/the-national-minimum-wage-in-2026/the-national-minimum-wage-in-2026)).
- **National Minimum Wage (aged 18 to 20):** £10.85 per hour, up 85p (8.5%) from £10.00 ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/lpc-recommendations-take-the-national-living-wage-to-1271)).

These rates were given legal effect by the National Minimum Wage (Amendment) Regulations 2026, which came into force on 1 April 2026 ([legislation.gov.uk](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2026/357/made)). They apply from the first pay reference period beginning on or after that date ([lra.org.uk](https://www.lra.org.uk/hours-and-pay/pay-rates-glance-april-2026-2027)).

The rates change on 1 April each year, and the listed rates for April 2027 are £13.21 for those 21 and over and £11.27 for 18 to 20 year olds ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/national-minimum-wage-rates)).

The Social Security contribution and benefit base for 2026 is **$184,500**, up from $176,100 in 2025 ([govinfo.gov](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2025-11-03/html/2025-19763.htm)).

- **Employees and employers:** each pays 6.2% on earnings up to $184,500 ([irs.gov](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p15)). That makes the maximum employee withholding $11,439.00 ([ssa.gov](https://www.ssa.gov/employer/efw/26efw2.pdf)).
- **Self-employed:** the rate is 12.4% on earnings up to $184,500 ([ssa.gov](https://www.ssa.gov/pubs/EN-05-10003.pdf)).
- **Medicare:** there is no wage base limit, so all covered wages are subject to the 1.45% Medicare tax ([irs.gov](https://www.irs.gov/taxtopics/tc751)).

**$24,500.** A 401(k) participant may defer no more than $24,500 of salary in 2026, or 100% of compensation if that is lower.

Savers get $1,000 more room than in 2025, when the ceiling stood at $23,500. Traditional pre-tax and Roth 401(k) deferrals count together against that one limit.
